tldr: This paper proposes a spatial semantic communication system that integrates index modulation with joint source-channel coding for efficient digital semantic transmission.
motivation: Current digital semantic communication systems rely on conventional constellation-based modulation, which is less spectrally and energy-efficient than index modulation.
method: The system uses fluid antenna index modulation (FA-IM) and residual quantization (RQ) to discretize analog semantic features, with a semantic-aware stream splitting scheme to protect critical information.
result: Simulations show that the proposed system achieves high fidelity, reliability, and spatial efficiency, outperforming traditional approaches.
conclusion: The SSC system provides a robust solution for future digital semantic transmission by synergizing RQ, semantic-aware splitting, and FA-IM.

title: Examining Qrmi As A Unified Interface For Quantum-HPC Integration
authors: Thomas Badts (pasqal), Tim Boyle (national Quantum Computing Centre), Claudio Carvalho (IBM), Antonio C\'orcoles (IBM), Andrew Damin (rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Vadim Elisseev (IBM), Jonathan Frassineti (CINECA), Daniel Gruber (HPC Gridware), Hiroshi Horii (IBM), Eun-Kyung Lee (IBM), James Machin (alice & Bob), Sara Marzella (CINECA), Mateusz Meller (STFC Hartree Centre), Daniel Milroy (lawrence Livermore National Laboratory), Matthieu Moreau (pasqal), Munetaka Ohtani (IBM), Elisabeth Ortega-Carrasco (qilimanjaro Quantum Tech), Doug Oucharek (oak Ridge National Laboratory), Yoonho Park (IBM), Adarsh Patil (siemens), Emre M. Sahin (STFC Hartree Centre), G\'abor Samu (IBM), Seetharami Seelam (IBM), Amir Shehata (oak Ridge National Laboratory), Vanessa Sochat (lawrence Livermore National Laboratory), James Thorne (national Quantum Computing Centre), Oscar Wallis (STFC Hartree Centre), Aleksander Wennersteen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The efficient and scalable integration of quantum resources into high-performance computing (HPC) environments requires standardized mechanisms for resource management, scheduling, and workflow orchestration across diverse and heterogeneous infrastructures. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) addresses this challenge through a thin, vendor-agnostic middleware layer that provides standardized APIs for scheduling, executing, and monitoring quantum workloads while exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs. Although previous work demonstrated QRMI integration with the Slurm workload manager, its applicability across other workload managers remained unexamined. This paper extends the validation of QRMI to a broad range of workload managers, including PBS, LSF, Grid Engine, Kubernetes, and the Flux Framework, encompassing traditional batch schedulers, a cloud-native orchestration platform, and a graph-based scheduler. We examine the integration patterns, implementation requirements, and scheduler-specific considerations associated with each environment and compare QRMI with alternative approaches to quantum resource integration. We demonstrate that QRMI provides a portable and flexible abstraction layer that minimizes scheduler-specific modifications while enabling consistent access to heterogeneous quantum resources across both on-premises and cloud environments.
tldr: This paper validates the Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) across multiple workload managers for quantum-HPC integration.
motivation: Efficient integration of quantum resources into HPC environments requires standardized resource management and scheduling mechanisms.
method: The authors extend QRMI validation to various workload managers (PBS, LSF, Grid Engine, Kubernetes, Flux Framework) and compare integration patterns.
result: QRMI provides a portable abstraction layer that minimizes scheduler-specific modifications while enabling consistent access to heterogeneous quantum resources.
conclusion: QRMI is a viable middleware for quantum-HPC integration across diverse HPC environments.

title: Information Propagation And Contraction In Functional Interpretations
authors: Chuangjie Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper separates two components of functional interpretations: affine information propagation and contraction. We introduce information nuclei as an algebraic interface to capture the affine component. An information nucleus specifies what information is associated with finite-type objects, how exact objects are compatible with such information, and how information is propagated through functions. From any information nucleus we obtain a formula translation and a soundness theorem for affine finite-type arithmetic. Extending soundness to finite-type arithmetic with contraction requires one additional ingredient: a formula-indexed contraction structure reducing the challenges generated by duplicated assumptions to a single challenge. Finite collections of candidates with union yield a Herbrand-style interpretation, while exact information with challenge selection yields the usual Dialectica interpretation over an arithmetic system restricted to decidable primitive formulas. The resulting framework provides a uniform method for specifying the information carried by extracted realizers, allowing existing functional interpretations to be systematically enriched with auxiliary data, such as continuity information.
tldr: This paper develops a framework for functional interpretations in logic, separating affine information propagation and contraction.
motivation: To provide a uniform method for specifying information carried by extracted realizers in functional interpretations, enabling systematic enrichment with auxiliary data.
method: Introduces information nuclei as an algebraic interface for affine information propagation, and formula-indexed contraction structures to handle contraction in finite-type arithmetic.
result: The framework yields a Herbrand-style interpretation and a Dialectica interpretation over decidable primitive formulas, allowing enrichment with continuity information.
conclusion: The work offers a modular approach to functional interpretations but is primarily a contribution to proof theory and logic, not directly related to quantum information theory or the other specified directions.

title: Quantum Term Rewrite Systems: Applications To Complexity Analysis
authors: Kostia Chardonnet, Emmanuel Hainry, Romain P\'echoux, Thomas Vinet
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Term Rewrite Systems (TRS) is a computational model offering a level of abstraction well-suited towards static analysis, e.g., termination or complexity analyses. In this paper, we introduce Quantum Term Rewrite Systems (QTRS), an extension of TRS to quantum computing, thus allowing to benefit from quantum advantage while being able to certify the complexity. We ensure that QTRS correspond to physically realizable processes and adapt techniques to obtain termination certificates or generic bounds on the reduction length. We delineate a class of terminating QTRS that can be compiled to uniform families of quantum circuits of size bounded by the reduction length. Conversely, this class is universal for quantum circuits. In particular, we show a characterization of the class of functions computable in quantum polynomial time, known as [MATH].
tldr: This paper extends term rewrite systems to quantum computing for complexity analysis, but does not align with the user's research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to combine quantum computing with term rewrite systems to certify complexity and termination, leveraging quantum advantage.
method: They introduce Quantum Term Rewrite Systems (QTRS), define a class of terminating QTRS that can be compiled to uniform families of quantum circuits, and show universality for quantum circuits.
result: The paper characterizes the class of functions computable in quantum polynomial time using QTRS.
conclusion: QTRS provide a framework for complexity analysis of quantum algorithms, but the work is more about computational models than the user's specific interests.

title: Dynamic Logic With Parallel Operator For Verifying Communication Protocols
authors: Mario R. F. Benevides Luiz C. F. Fernandez (federal University Of Rio de Janeiro)
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a dynamic logic with parallel operators for the formal verification of authenticity and safety properties of cryptographic protocols. The logic incorporates communication actions and is specifically designed to reason about protocol executions in adversarial environments. We extend an existing dynamic logic with parallel operators by introducing concepts derived from the Dolev-Yao intruder model. As the underlying logic is completely axiomatizable, we obtain a complete axiomatization for the extended system. Furthermore, we develop a tableau calculus for the proposed logic and prove its termination, soundness, and completeness.
tldr: This paper presents a dynamic logic with parallel operators for verifying communication protocols, focusing on cryptographic protocol security.
motivation: To formally verify authenticity and safety properties of cryptographic protocols in adversarial environments using a logical framework.
method: Extends an existing dynamic logic with parallel operators and incorporates concepts from the Dolev-Yao intruder model, providing a complete axiomatization and a tableau calculus.
result: Obtains a complete axiomatization for the extended system and proves termination, soundness, and completeness of the tableau calculus.
conclusion: The proposed logic enables formal verification of communication protocols, but the work is primarily in logic and protocol verification, not directly aligned with the user's research interests.

title: From Dag-Like Proofs To Boolean Circuits In Lean
authors: Edward Hermann Haeusler Lorenzo Saraiva (pontificia Universidade Catolica Do Rio de Janeiro)
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we present a method for encoding Dag-Like Derivability Structures (DLDS), obtained via horizontal compression of Natural Deduction proofs in purely implicational minimal logic, as Boolean circuits. These DLDS compress Natural Deduction tree-like proofs into directed acyclic graphs, preserving logical correctness while reducing redundancy. We formally define the circuit construction process and establish its pointwise correctness, showing that, for any fixed path assignment, the resulting Boolean circuit agrees with the intended dependency-propagation semantics. A Lean formalization establishes machine-checked guarantees for the circuit evaluator and includes a restricted bridge for the uncompressed simple-tree fragment, connecting valid DLDS instances in that fragment to genuine circuit acceptance of their extracted paths under the route and discharge conditions formalized in Lean. This approach opens new perspectives for automated theorem proving and formal certification.
tldr: This paper encodes Dag-Like Derivability Structures from natural deduction proofs into Boolean circuits and formalizes the construction in Lean.
motivation: To reduce redundancy in natural deduction proofs and enable automated theorem proving with machine-checked guarantees.
method: The authors define a horizontal compression of tree-like proofs into directed acyclic graphs (DLDS) and then construct Boolean circuits from these DLDS, proving pointwise correctness.
result: A Lean formalization provides machine-checked guarantees for the circuit evaluator and a restricted bridge for the simple-tree fragment.
conclusion: This approach opens new perspectives for automated theorem proving and formal certification, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Synthesizing Superoscillations With Just Two Frequencies
authors: Diyar Talbayev Denys I. Bondar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superoscillations, band-limited signals that locally oscillate faster than their highest Fourier component, have recently enabled superspectroscopy and super-sensing. Previous experiments [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 153803 (2023), [URL] and APL Photonics 10, 086107 (2025), [URL] relied on combining four quasi-sinusoidal harmonics to generate temporal superoscillations. Here, we show that just two harmonics are sufficient to produce superoscillations of comparable quality, as quantified by the local frequency. By reanalyzing prior experimental data with two harmonics (0.5 and 0.6 THz) and performing new experiments with 0.9 and 1 THz harmonics, we demonstrate a twofold enhancement in local frequency relative to the highest frequency component -- matching the enhancement previously achieved with four harmonics. We provide a simple analytical explanation for the bichromatic superoscillations based on near-complete destructive interference, and identify an optimal frequency separation of approximately 10% that balances the superoscillatory frequency enhancement against signal amplitude. This simplification substantially lowers the experimental barrier to implementing superoscillation-based technology.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that superoscillations can be synthesized using just two frequencies, achieving comparable quality to previous four-frequency experiments.
motivation: Superoscillations enable super-resolution sensing and spectroscopy, but previous implementations required multiple harmonics, increasing experimental complexity. The authors aim to simplify the generation of superoscillations.
method: The authors reanalyze prior experimental data and perform new experiments using two harmonics (0.5/0.6 THz and 0.9/1 THz), and provide an analytical explanation based on near-complete destructive interference.
result: Bichromatic superoscillations achieve a twofold enhancement in local frequency relative to the highest frequency component, matching the enhancement previously achieved with four harmonics. An optimal frequency separation of ~10% is identified.
conclusion: Superoscillations can be generated with just two frequencies, significantly lowering the experimental barrier for superoscillation-based technologies.

title: Controllable Localization And Manipulation Of Optical Hollow Traps By Means Of Optical-vortex Diffraction
authors: O. V. Angelsky, A. Y. Bekshaev, C. Y. Zenkova, I. I. Mokhun, X. Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An optical vortex (OV) is coupled with the local intensity zero and is thus a field configuration suitable for "hollow" optical traps and optical tweezers. When an incident circular OV beam experiences diffraction at a rectilinear screen edge (SE), and the conditions of weak diffraction perturbation (the SE is far enough from the beam axis) are fulfilled, the main consequence is the OV-core displacement from its initial (axial) position. Based on the model of incident Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) beam, we investigate analytically and numerically the ways of controlling the OV-core position in the diffracted-field cross section by means of changing the SE position with respect to the incident-beam axis. The results show that regulating the SE position with ~1 mcm accuracy (which is available for existing mechanical tools), controllable OV-core motion with a sub-nanometer accuracy can be realized. Possible modifications of this motion depending on the incident beam topological charge, wavefront curvature, SE properties (semitransparent screen, phase-step screen) and the distance between the diffraction plane and the observation plane are analyzed. The conditions most favorable for the micro-object trapping and manipulation are specified and discussed.
tldr: This paper studies the controllable displacement of an optical vortex core via diffraction at a screen edge, enabling sub-nanometer precision for optical trapping.
motivation: Optical vortices with intensity zeros are useful for hollow optical traps, but controlling the vortex core position with high precision is challenging.
method: Analytical and numerical modeling of a Laguerre-Gaussian beam diffracted at a rectilinear screen edge, varying screen position, topological charge, wavefront curvature, and screen properties.
result: Regulating the screen edge position with ~1 μm accuracy enables controllable vortex core motion with sub-nanometer accuracy.
conclusion: The proposed method allows precise manipulation of optical hollow traps, which is promising for micro-object trapping and manipulation.

title: Toroidal Transitions In Hydrogenic And Alkali Atoms
authors: Kai Xiang Lee, Vincent Mancois, Kelvin Lim, David Wilkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In addition to electric and magnetic multipoles, the expansion of current density also yields toroidal terms, a lesser-known family of multipoles. A recent proposal, I. Kuprov [MATH], Science Adv. 8 abq6751 (2022), explores the possibility of a direct observation of optical toroidal transitions in hydrogen and alkali atoms in the presence of a large magnetic field that decouples the spin and the angular momentum of the electron. However, the difficulty of observing these transitions against the nearby electric dipole (E1) transitions were underestimated because of extra admixture coming from diamagnetic coupling. Here, we revisit the toroidal coupling in atoms, taking diamagnetic contribution into account, and discuss the technical challenges of observing toroidal coupling in atomic physics. We show that toroidal transition should be searched in transitions with low principal quantum numbers. The remaining strong electric-dipole contribution could be removed using an appropriate differential measurement.
tldr: This paper studies toroidal transitions in hydrogenic and alkali atoms, focusing on atomic physics and spectroscopy.
motivation: To revisit the feasibility of observing optical toroidal transitions in atoms, which were previously proposed but underestimated due to diamagnetic coupling.
method: The authors analyze the toroidal coupling in atoms including diamagnetic contributions, and identify transitions with low principal quantum numbers where toroidal effects may be observable.
result: They show that toroidal transitions should be searched in low principal quantum number transitions, and that strong electric-dipole contributions can be removed via differential measurements.
conclusion: Observing toroidal transitions in atoms remains challenging but possible with careful experimental design.

title: Combinatorial Capacity Bounds For The $q$-ary Deletion Channel
authors: Hassan Tavakoli, Thinh Nguyen, Bella Bose
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the \(q\)-ary deletion channel via the pattern-count scalar \(N_n(x,y)\), the number of deletion subsets mapping \(x\in\Sigma_q^n\) to \(y\in\Sigma_q^k\), which factorizes the transition probability. Two sum identities on \(N_n\) certify stochastic normalization and, under uniform input, yield an exact closed-form output entropy. These give the finite-block capacity sandwich \( (1-d)\log_2 q-h_2(d)\;\le\; C_{q,n}\;\le\;(1-d)\log_2 q. \) The exact uniform-input rate is \( {n}I_U(X;Y) =(1-d)\log_2 q+{n}H_{}(n,1-d)-h_2(d)+{n}, \) from which the simpler certified bound \( C_{q,n}\ge (1-d)\log_2 q-h_2(d)+{n} \) follows. The small-\(d\) bound \(C_q(d)\ge\log_2 q+d\log_2 d+O(d)\) follows for all \(q\ge 2\). Numerical experiments at \(n=3,5,10\) and \(q=2,3\) confirm all bounds.
tldr: The paper derives combinatorial capacity bounds for the q-ary deletion channel using pattern-count scalars.
motivation: Understanding the capacity of deletion channels is a fundamental problem in classical information theory, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors introduce a pattern-count scalar N_n(x,y) that factorizes the transition probability, and derive sum identities to obtain exact output entropy under uniform input.
result: They obtain finite-block capacity bounds: (1-d)log2 q - h2(d) ≤ C_{q,n} ≤ (1-d)log2 q, and a small-d bound C_q(d) ≥ log2 q + d log2 d + O(d).
conclusion: The bounds are tight for small deletion probabilities and confirmed numerically, but the work is purely classical and not relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Bounds And Limitations On Codes Achieving List Recovery Capacity
authors: Joshua Brakensiek, Yeyuan Chen, Aaron Putterman, Zihan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In coding theory, list recoverability is a fundamental concept which robustly captures how ``spread-out'' codewords are in a code. More formally, given a code [MATH] and input lists [MATH] of size at most [MATH], list recoverability requires that there are at most [MATH] codewords [MATH] such that [MATH] for at least [MATH] choices of [MATH]. List recovery is an important question which has found applications in many areas, including complexity theory, property testing, compressed sensing, streaming algorithms, and cryptography. As our first main result, we establish a tight ``generalized singleton bound''. Formally, we show that for constant [MATH] and sufficiently large alphabets [MATH], if we define [MATH], it is possible for a [MATH] list-recoverable code to have rate [MATH] but impossible to have rate [MATH]. One direction of our result already directly generalizes and improves a weaker impossibility result due to Goldberg, Shangguan, and Tamo. For our second main result, we prove that there is a fundamental shortcoming in existing methods that aim to construct explicit, optimal list-recoverable codes. Indeed, recent work has constructed explicit codes achieving list-decoding capacity (along with other related properties) using a framework introduced in the work of Alon--Edmonds--Luby (AEL). We give a meta-analysis of such constructions by presenting an ``AEL framework'' which captures all such recent constructions in the literature. motivation: List recoverability is a fundamental concept in coding theory with applications in complexity theory, property testing, and cryptography. The paper aims to establish optimal rate bounds and understand limitations of current construction frameworks.
method: The authors prove a tight generalized Singleton bound for list-recoverable codes over large alphabets, and provide a meta-analysis of the Alon-Edmonds-Luby (AEL) framework to show that no AEL-based construction can achieve optimal list-recovery capacity for additive and linear codes.

conclusion: The results provide fundamental limits on list-recoverable codes and highlight the need for new construction methods beyond the AEL framework.

title: Learning To Transmit: Volatility-Aware Predictive Communication For Energy-Efficient IoT Networks
authors: John Kangethe, Ifrat Ikhtear Uddin, Longwei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication is the dominant source of energy consumption in Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks, yet many sensed measurements exhibit strong temporal correlations and provide little new information to the receiver. This paper introduces , a volatility-aware predictive communication framework that enables IoT devices to intelligently decide when communication is necessary. Each sensor maintains a lightweight machine learning predictor and transmits only when the prediction residual exceeds an adaptive threshold proportional to the local signal volatility. By normalizing prediction errors using a rolling estimate of signal variability, the proposed transmission policy automatically adapts to changing environmental conditions, seasonal variations, and deployment-specific dynamics without manual threshold tuning. To address long-term non-stationarity, we further propose , an online learning extension based on Recursive Least Squares (RLS) with exponential forgetting, allowing continuous adaptation to sensor drift and evolving signal characteristics. Extensive experiments are conducted on three heterogeneous real-world datasets comprising more than 2.4 million sensor observations from outdoor environmental monitoring, indoor wireless sensor networks, and urban air-quality sensing. Compared with six representative baselines, including periodic transmission, static-threshold suppression, ARIMA, Kalman filtering, EMA, and LMS filtering, achieves up to 94.7\% transmission reduction while maintaining a reconstruction error of 0.352[MATH]C. further reduces reconstruction error by 12--18\% under drift conditions while preserving transmission reduction above 93\%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of volatility-aware predictive communication for energy-efficient and adaptive IoT networks.
tldr: A volatility-aware predictive communication framework for energy-efficient IoT networks that reduces transmission by up to 94.7% while maintaining low reconstruction error.
motivation: Communication is the dominant energy consumer in IoT networks, yet many sensor measurements are temporally correlated and provide little new information, necessitating an adaptive transmission policy.
method: Each sensor uses a lightweight machine learning predictor and transmits only when the prediction residual exceeds an adaptive threshold proportional to local signal volatility; an online learning extension based on Recursive Least Squares with exponential forgetting handles non-stationarity.
result: On three real-world datasets, the framework achieves up to 94.7% transmission reduction with reconstruction error of 0.352°C, and the online extension reduces error by 12–18% under drift while maintaining >93% reduction.
conclusion: Volatility-aware predictive communication is effective for energy-efficient and adaptive IoT networks, significantly reducing transmissions without sacrificing data fidelity.

title: Relative Entropy Analysis Of The Jin-Xin Model: Theory And Numerics
authors: Christina Mahmoud
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work studies the linear Jin-Xin relaxation model by means of the relative entropy method, both at the continuous and fully discrete levels. Under the strict subcharacteristic condition, we obtain an O([MATH]) estimate for the convergence toward the equilibrium transport equation. We then develop discrete relative entropy estimates for a Lie splitting scheme and an asymptotic preserving staggered scheme. A fixed-time analysis further explains the O([MATH]^2 ) behavior observed in the strongly stiff regime and the transition occurring when [MATH] becomes comparable to the time step.
tldr: This paper studies the linear Jin-Xin relaxation model using relative entropy methods at continuous and discrete levels.
motivation: The Jin-Xin model is a hyperbolic relaxation system; understanding its convergence to equilibrium is important for numerical schemes.
method: Relative entropy estimates are derived under the strict subcharacteristic condition for the continuous model and for two numerical schemes (Lie splitting and an asymptotic preserving staggered scheme).
result: An O(ε) convergence rate is obtained for the continuous model, and discrete estimates explain O(ε^2) behavior in the stiff regime.
conclusion: The relative entropy method provides a unified framework for analyzing the Jin-Xin model and its numerical approximations.

title: On Runlength Limited Codes For Bicm Systems
authors: Stephan Zeitz, Florian Roth, Meik D\"orpinghaus, Gerhard Fettweis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the use of runlength-limited (RLL) block codes in bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) systems. In this setting, the RLL code acts as the symbol mapper, whose assignment between input bits and RLL symbols is critical for performance. In this work, we aim at optimizing the assignment scheme of RLL codes. One of the main applications of RLL codes is the mitigation of intersymbol interference (ISI) in systems with coarse quantization. However, channel memory and quantization nonlinearity complicate information theoretic analysis. To enable analytical treatment, we consider a block channel with 1-bit analog-to-digital conversion, modeling the transmission of a single RLL code block. For this channel, we investigate the relationship between the achievable rate in BICM systems-termed BICM capacity-and the RLL code's assignment scheme. Focusing on low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), we derive the optimization problem yielding the optimal assignment scheme. By looking at asymptotically large block-lengths, we infer a practical optimization strategy for RLL codes with finite block-length and channels with inter-block interference. Further, we extend this optimization to two-state RLL (TS-RLL) codes, which offer higher code rates than state independent RLL codes. We demonstrate that optimized TS-RLL codes exhibit significant performance improvements over literature counterparts.
tldr: This paper studies runlength-limited block codes for bit-interleaved coded modulation systems, focusing on optimizing the assignment scheme to improve performance in channels with coarse quantization.
motivation: Runlength-limited codes are used to mitigate intersymbol interference in systems with coarse quantization, but the assignment between input bits and RLL symbols critically affects performance and lacks optimization.
method: The authors model a block channel with 1-bit analog-to-digital conversion and derive an optimization problem for the assignment scheme at low SNRs, extending to two-state RLL codes and finite block-lengths.
result: Optimized assignment schemes for RLL and two-state RLL codes are derived, showing significant performance improvements over literature counterparts.
conclusion: The proposed optimization strategy for RLL code assignment enhances BICM system performance, particularly in low-SNR regimes with coarse quantization.

title: Robust Classification In Ml: A Topological Semantics Approach
authors: Mirko Tagliaferri Dominik Pichler (TU Wien)
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust classification is commonly understood as the stability of a classifier under small perturbations (often adversarial) of input data. In this paper, we propose a logical framework for robust classification grounded in topological semantics for modal logic. Evaluation points are feature vectors representing machine-readable objects, and formulas express explicit classifications. Robustness is interpreted geometrically as local truth persistence: a classification is robust at a point if it holds throughout some non-empty open neighbourhood of that point. Building on this perspective, we introduce a logical language with a robustness modality interpreted over S4 topological spaces, together with a robustness-sensitive conditional connective. This conditional connective captures global inclusion relations between robust regions and other properties of the classifier: it holds at a point when the neighbourhood witnessing the robustness of one formula is contained in the truth set of another. In this way, robust classifications can be systematically linked to classification conditions. We provide a sound and complete axiomatisation of the resulting logic. Finally, we introduce Minimal Robust Models, a constructive method for generating models from specified robustness constraints, which yields formal tools for analysing, explaining, and structuring robust classification behaviour.
tldr: This paper proposes a logical framework for robust classification in machine learning using topological semantics for modal logic.
motivation: Robust classification is important for stability under adversarial perturbations, but existing approaches lack a formal logical foundation.
method: The authors introduce a modal logic with a robustness modality interpreted over S4 topological spaces, and define a robustness-sensitive conditional connective to capture global inclusion relations.
result: They provide a sound and complete axiomatization of the logic and introduce Minimal Robust Models for constructing models from robustness constraints.
conclusion: The framework offers formal tools for analyzing and explaining robust classification behavior, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: New Lower Bounds For Binary Constant-weight Codes: $A(23,6,10)\geq 2979$ And $A(24,6,10)\geq 4214$
authors: Christian Lysenstoeen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] denote the maximum size of a binary constant-weight code of length [MATH], minimum distance [MATH], and weight [MATH]. We construct explicit codes proving [MATH] and [MATH]. These improve the best surviving explicit codes of sizes 2969 and 4174 and surpass the corresponding 1990 bounds 2970 and 4200 of Brouwer, Shearer, Sloane and Smith, whose code listings were lost. We also obtain [MATH] and [MATH]. All four bounds are now listed in Brouwer's online table. The constructions use a coordinate decomposition in which one half is fixed to a known code and the complementary half is selected from its full cross-compatible pool using CHILS for maximum-weight independent set. For the 2969-word [MATH] incumbent, exact computations with two solver families prove insertion maximality and exclude every improving exchange deleting at most three codewords. tldr: This paper presents new lower bounds for binary constant-weight codes using combinatorial constructions and computational search.
motivation: Improving bounds for constant-weight codes is a classic problem in coding theory with applications in communication and storage.
method: The authors use a coordinate decomposition method combined with maximum-weight independent set (CHILS) and exact computational solvers to construct and verify codes.
result: New lower bounds A(23,6,10) ≥ 2979 and A(24,6,10) ≥ 4214 are established, surpassing previous records.
