title: Inference-Behaviour Semantics For All$^\ast$ Connectives In Two-Dimensional Sequent Calculi
authors: Sophie Nagler
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-behaviour semantics (I-bS) is a new approach to proof-theoretic semantics, grounded in two inferentialist principles: (1) the use of an expression in reasoning determines its meaning, and (2) a connective is defined by its operational rules. I-bS operationalises these ideas by measuring the syntactic use of a connective in the proof of its definability, against a substructurally minimal derivability relation. I-bS thereby gives the meaning of a connective in terms of its semantic clause, i.e. minimal substructural rule pair. This paper validates and verifies I-bS by applying it to all [MATH] connective rule pairs that can be formulated in two-dimensional sequent calculi using at most two premiss sequents and at most two active formulae. As a result, we find semantic clauses for exactly [MATH] meaningful connectives, namely bottom, top, two negations (intuitionistic and dual-intuitionistic), group and lattice conjunction, disjunction and implication, as well as their converses and inverses. We use these results to precisely map the semantic interrelations among the connectives, across linear, classical, intuitionistic, dual-intuitionistic, minimal, and lattice logic. Most notably, we find that intuitionistic negation, disjunction and implication each capture half of the meaning of their classical counterparts.
tldr: This paper presents inference-behaviour semantics for all connectives in two-dimensional sequent calculi, a proof-theoretic semantics approach.
motivation: To provide a new approach to proof-theoretic semantics that measures the syntactic use of connectives in proofs to define their meaning.
method: The paper applies inference-behaviour semantics to all connective rule pairs in two-dimensional sequent calculi with at most two premises and two active formulae, deriving semantic clauses.
result: Semantic clauses for 16 meaningful connectives are found, including bottom, top, two negations, group and lattice conjunction, disjunction, implication, and their converses and inverses.
conclusion: The results map semantic interrelations among connectives across various logics, showing that intuitionistic negation, disjunction, and implication each capture half the meaning of their classical counterparts.

title: JailMeter: An Evidence-Based Evaluation Framework For Jailbreak Attacks On Large Language Models
authors: Qingjia Huang, Jingyu Zhang, Jianguo Wu, Yakai Li, Weijuan Zhang, Yankai Rong, Junyi Yao, Shengzhi Zhang, Xiaoqi Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The assessment of jailbreak attacks against large language models currently suffers from inconsistent evaluation criteria and methods, leading to unreliable estimates of attack success rates. We propose JailMeter, an evidence-based evaluation framework designed to more faithfully measure jailbreak effectiveness. Inspired by the Information Bottleneck theory, JailMeter applies dual-feedback optimization to filter jailbreak noise from model responses while preserving content relevant to the original malicious question. This process produces concise evidence for a rigorous assessment under which an attack is validated only when the response captures the malicious intent and delivers a complete answer, thereby signaling a substantive bypass of model safety alignment. We evaluate JailMeter on JailMeter-Eva, a challenging benchmark containing 330 human-labeled, non-rejected jailbreak instances. JailMeter achieves an accuracy of 97.27%, substantially outperforming existing evaluation methods. To support large-scale evaluation, we further distill JailMeter into a small language model, JailMeter, which maintains comparable reliability with significantly reduced computational costs. Code and dataset are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes an evidence-based evaluation framework for jailbreak attacks on large language models, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Current evaluation of jailbreak attacks lacks consistent criteria, leading to unreliable success rate estimates.
method: JailMeter uses dual-feedback optimization inspired by Information Bottleneck theory to filter noise and extract concise evidence from model responses.
result: JailMeter achieves 97.27% accuracy on a human-labeled benchmark, outperforming existing methods.
conclusion: The framework provides a more faithful and scalable evaluation of jailbreak attacks.

title: ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose Into Safe Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Elias Hossain, Md Mehedi Hasan Nipu, Fatema Tuj Johora Faria, Tasfia Nuzhat Ornee, Maleeha Sheikh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, and every hop between agents is an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, SmoothLLM) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. We show this gap carries a consequence rarely measured: on a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, an undefended pipeline that appears fully safe under standard reporting (attack success 0.000 on tool- and memory-poisoning) owes that safety almost entirely to the cloud provider's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks on Azure GPT-5), and silently shifts to the agent model's own alignment on a backend without such a filter. Outcome-only reporting hides this dependence. We present ChannelGuard, a training-free defense-in-depth framework placing information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel; each scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank by embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it, adding no LLM call, while an attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, whereas the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends; it also lowers Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline does better. An extended appendix adds baselines, ablations, sweeps, a benign-preservation analysis, and a judge audit (kappa = 0.900), at a total cost of 47.36 USD.
tldr: This paper proposes a defense framework for multi-agent LLM systems against adversarial instruction smuggling, but is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Existing defenses for multi-agent LLM pipelines only guard input boundaries or rely on opaque provider-side filters, leaving inter-agent channels vulnerable to attacks.
method: ChannelGuard places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel, scoring text against an adversarial phrase bank via embedding similarity and deterministically passing, compressing, or blocking it.
result: ChannelGuard blocks tool poisoning 30/30 across backends, reduces prompt injection success from 0.333 to 0.167, and preserves GSM8K accuracy at 0.867, but is evaded by white-box adaptive paraphrases.
conclusion: ChannelGuard provides a training-free defense-in-depth for multi-agent LLM systems, but the paper is entirely about LLM security and has no connection to quantum information theory.

title: ChainWatch: A Kill Chain-Aligned Sequential Detection Framework For Multi-Step Attacks In MCP-Based Ai Agent Systems
authors: Om Narayan, Rashmi Jyoti, Ramkinker Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard that allows AI agents to connect to external tools, databases, and services. While this connectivity enables powerful agent capabilities, it also introduces multi-step attacks that existing per-call defenses cannot reliably detect. Attackers can compose individually benign tool invocations into malicious sequences that evade isolated inspection. This paper presents ChainWatch, a sequential detection framework for identifying multi-step attacks in MCP-based AI agent systems. ChainWatch models attack progression using a six-stage kill chain and applies a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to classify tool-call sequences. Detection rules are triggered when a session exhibits suspicious progression across multiple stages. The framework is supported by a structured threat model covering direct sequential attacks, indirect prompt injection chains, and hybrid multi-stage attacks. A 20-dimensional feature extraction schema captures behavioral signals from tool interactions. We demonstrate the approach using five representative attack scenarios from the security literature, showing how ChainWatch detects attack chains that evade traditional per-call security mechanisms.
tldr: This paper presents a sequential detection framework for multi-step attacks in AI agent systems using the Model Context Protocol.
motivation: Existing per-call defenses cannot detect multi-step attacks where individually benign tool invocations form malicious sequences.
method: ChainWatch models attack progression with a six-stage kill chain and uses a Hidden Markov Model to classify tool-call sequences, supported by a 20-dimensional feature extraction schema.
result: The framework is demonstrated on five attack scenarios, showing detection of attack chains that evade traditional per-call security mechanisms.
conclusion: ChainWatch provides a structured approach to detect multi-step attacks in MCP-based AI agent systems.

title: Building Trust In Autonomous Commerce: A Verifiable Global Event Timeline And AI-Ready Fraud Intelligence Layer
authors: Rajat Srivastava
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic commerce protocols such as AP2 and ACP define mechanisms for secure agent-initiated transactions but do not provide interoperable, tamper-evident auditability or verifiable temporal ordering of events across heterogeneous domains. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing a verifiable global event timeline for agentic commerce, constructed from four core components: canonical event schemas that enforce deterministic serialization, deterministic batch formation ensuring reproducible ordering without reliance on synchronized clocks, Merkle-based append-only commitments providing logarithmic-cost inclusion proofs, and blockchain anchoring establishing a tamper-evident temporal backbone. Building on this infrastructure, we introduce a cryptographically signed fraud marker that binds risk labels to anchored evidence through an unforgeable provenance chain, and a dataset lineage model enabling reproducible, tamper-evident AI training pipelines. Empirical results from a prototype implementation demonstrate: Merkle tree construction processes 50,000 events in 47 milliseconds; end-to-end verification completes in under 0.013 milliseconds regardless of batch size; inclusion proof sizes grow logarithmically from 320 bytes at 1,000 events to 512 bytes at 50,000 events; and Merkle-based verification outperforms linear scan by 14.4x at 50,000 events.
tldr: This paper proposes a verifiable global event timeline and fraud intelligence layer for agentic commerce, using Merkle trees and blockchain anchoring.
motivation: Current agentic commerce protocols lack interoperable, tamper-evident auditability and verifiable temporal ordering across heterogeneous domains.
method: The system uses canonical event schemas, deterministic batch formation, Merkle-based append-only commitments, and blockchain anchoring to create a tamper-evident timeline, along with cryptographically signed fraud markers and dataset lineage models.
result: A prototype processes 50,000 events in 47 ms, end-to-end verification in under 0.013 ms, and inclusion proofs grow logarithmically; Merkle-based verification outperforms linear scan by 14.4x at 50,000 events.
conclusion: The proposed infrastructure provides efficient, scalable, and tamper-evident auditability for agentic commerce, enabling trust in autonomous transactions.

title: When Http 402 Meets The Blockchain: Risks On Emerging X402 Payments
authors: Qinying Wang, Yong Yang, Yuan Chen, Shouling Ji, Mathias Payer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: x402 is an emerging payment protocol for Web APIs and autonomous AI agents. x402 extends HTTP 402 with a payment negotiation flow and delegates payment proof verification and on-chain settlement to third-party facilitators. As a result, facilitators serve as a shared payment infrastructure for many independent merchants. This centralizes trust and validation in one component, so a single flaw can affect many services. Despite rapid adoption by major vendors and economically meaningful mainnet activity, the security posture of real-world x402 deployments remains poorly characterized. We present the first systematic study of authorization correctness and execution safety in current facilitator-mediated x402 deployments in the wild, identifying eight security rules for facilitators as critical payment infrastructure. Based on our analysis of rule violations, we derive four new attack vectors, including Free Shopping, Asset Theft, Service Denial, and Gas Abuse. These attacks exploit weaknesses in the real-world facilitator and server implementations and cause severe harm, including direct financial loss to merchants, theft of facilitator-held assets, unbounded sponsor-paid gas/fees, and disruption of payment services. To assess the security of x402 deployments at scale, we propose a semi-automated black-box tool and apply it to 15 major x402 facilitators collectively used by over 60K sellers and 360K buyers. Alarmingly, we find violations in all evaluated facilitators. We responsibly disclosed our findings to the affected parties, who acknowledged the issues and adopted mitigations, including changes by Coinbase. Finally, we complement our controlled testing with an empirical measurement of over 119 million recent Base and Solana transactions, quantifying x402 adoption, facilitator centralization, and ecosystem-level risk indicators.
tldr: This paper analyzes security vulnerabilities in the x402 payment protocol, which integrates HTTP 402 with blockchain for Web API payments.
motivation: Despite rapid adoption of x402 by major vendors, its security posture is poorly characterized, and centralized facilitators introduce systemic risks.
method: The authors derive eight security rules for facilitators, identify four attack vectors, and develop a semi-automated black-box tool to test 15 major facilitators.
result: All evaluated facilitators violated security rules, enabling attacks like Free Shopping and Asset Theft; empirical measurement of 119M transactions reveals centralization risks.
conclusion: The findings highlight critical security flaws in current x402 deployments, leading to mitigations by affected parties including Coinbase.

title: Twin Agent: Context Residual Compression For Privilege Separated Agents
authors: Zhanhao Hu, Dennis Jacob, Xiao Huang, Zhaorun Chen, Bo Li, David Wagner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to security risks, such as prompt injection attacks from untrusted context that manipulate downstream reasoning and tool use. Existing secure-by-design approaches mitigate this risk by separating untrusted observations from privileged execution and careful control of information flow, but often degrade utility and require extensive task-specific engineering. We thus propose Twin Agent, a general privilege separation design pattern inspired by residual coding in the agent context. Twin Agent consists of two nearly symmetric agents: an Explore Agent that inspects untrusted information and a Safe Agent that executes privileged actions. The Explore Agent is conditioned on the Safe Agent's current context and communicates only compact hints to the Safe Agent about the next action to take. This design reduces the information needed to preserve task utility and thus achieves a better security--utility tradeoff, which we empirically verify by measuring how utility and attack success change as the length of hints varies. We evaluate Twin Agent on long-horizon software engineering tasks with SWE-bench Lite and on heterogeneous multi-tool interaction tasks with AgentDojo and DecodingTrust-Agent. Across both benchmarks, Twin Agent preserves high task utility while preventing prompt injection attacks, outperforming both undefended agents and privilege separation baselines.
tldr: This paper proposes a privilege separation design pattern for LLM agents to defend against prompt injection attacks by using a residual coding approach between two agents.
motivation: LLM agents are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks from untrusted context, and existing secure-by-design approaches degrade utility or require extensive engineering.
method: Twin Agent uses an Explore Agent that inspects untrusted information and communicates compact hints to a Safe Agent, which executes privileged actions, inspired by residual coding.
result: The method preserves high task utility while preventing prompt injection attacks on SWE-bench Lite, AgentDojo, and DecodingTrust-Agent benchmarks.
conclusion: Twin Agent achieves a better security-utility tradeoff than undefended agents and privilege separation baselines.

title: GhostPrompt: Cross-Image Adversarial Prompt For Vision-Language Models
authors: Li Zeng, Zeyu Ye, Meng Xie, Hangtao Zhang, Xianlong Wang, Yanchun Li, Zhetao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to images or texts induce erroneous outputs. However, most text-based attacks are adapted from language-model-centric methods, in which the visual input is fixed during optimization, resulting in adversarial prompts that are tied to specific images and thus limiting their attack effectiveness. To this end, we first introduce a new research perspective: cross-image transferability for adversarial prompts. We then propose GhostPrompt, an adversarial prompt that is optimized once and reused to steer VLM outputs toward attacker-specified responses across diverse images. GhostPrompt employs a joint optimization that distills image-invariant adversarial features into the prompt by "worst-case" generation. Specifically, it alternates between constructing hard visual conditions for the current prompt and updating the prompt to remain effective under these conditions. Extensive experiments on prevalent VLMs verify that \ourmethod achieves an improvement of over 30% in attack success rates compared to state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines, while reducing computation time by ~70%. Our code is avalable at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes GhostPrompt, an adversarial prompt attack for vision-language models that achieves cross-image transferability.
motivation: Existing text-based adversarial attacks on VLMs are image-specific, limiting their effectiveness. The authors aim to create a single adversarial prompt that works across diverse images.
method: GhostPrompt uses a joint optimization that alternates between constructing hard visual conditions and updating the prompt to remain effective under those conditions, distilling image-invariant adversarial features.
result: GhostPrompt achieves over 30% improvement in attack success rates compared to state-of-the-art baselines while reducing computation time by ~70%.
conclusion: The proposed method demonstrates strong cross-image transferability and efficiency, highlighting vulnerabilities in VLMs.

title: An Automated Framework For Extracting Reachable Attack Chains From Cyber Threat Intelligence Reports
authors: Wenbo Hou, Ning Hu, Xueping Wang, Jiahao Gu, Wenjian Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports richly describe real-world attack processes, but their unstructured narratives cannot be directly used for automated attack-path reasoning. Existing CTI extraction methods focus on indicators, entities, or TTP labels without modeling the execution conditions and resulting states of each attack step, so the extracted knowledge supports neither state matching nor reachability analysis across multi-stage attack chains. This paper proposes an automated framework that extracts reachable attack chains by modeling each attack step as an attack unit of preconditions, an attack behavior, and postconditions. A multi-stage pipeline assisted by large language models (LLMs) extracts attack behavior skeletons, recovers their preconditions and postconditions, normalizes them into predefined predicates, and repairs broken dependencies; the resulting units are compiled into Datalog-style rules for attack-goal reachability reasoning. On a dataset of 20 CTI reports containing 334 human-validated annotated steps, our framework achieves higher annotated-step coverage than representative CTI extraction systems in recovering attack behaviors. Moreover, by explicitly generating preconditions and postconditions, it produces attack units that are more complete and consistent than those generated by end-to-end LLM baselines. On the extracted chains, Datalog inference reaches the specified attack goal in 19 of 20 reports, while backward search yields 34 attack paths under the generated rules. The source code and experimental artifacts are available in an anonymized repository. .
tldr: This paper presents an automated framework using LLMs to extract reachable attack chains from cyber threat intelligence reports.
motivation: CTI reports contain unstructured narratives that cannot be directly used for automated attack-path reasoning, and existing extraction methods lack modeling of execution conditions and states.
method: The framework models each attack step as an attack unit with preconditions, behavior, and postconditions, uses a multi-stage LLM pipeline to extract and normalize these units, and compiles them into Datalog rules for reachability reasoning.
result: On 20 CTI reports with 334 annotated steps, the framework achieves higher coverage than existing systems and produces more complete and consistent attack units, enabling Datalog inference to reach the specified goal in 19 of 20 reports.
conclusion: The framework effectively extracts structured attack chains from unstructured CTI reports, enabling automated reasoning about multi-stage attack paths.

title: Darwin: Evolving Jailbreak Adversary And Guardrail For Llm Safety Evaluation And Protection
authors: Weiwei Qi, Zefeng Wu, Zhilin Guo, Tianhang Zheng, Chaochao Lu, Liang He, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most existing LLM safety evaluation and defense methods follow a static formulation: jailbreak vulnerabilities are evaluated with fixed attack methods, and guardrails are trained on fixed malicious prompt datasets. However, real-world adversaries continuously evolve their capabilities and expand the attack space. To address this challenge, we propose DARWIN, an evolutionary attack-defense framework that formulates jailbreaking as an open-ended evolution process and continuously updates guardrails through an evolving attack-defense loop. DARWIN-Attack is an evolutionary adversary that expands its capabilities through strategy discovery, mutation, selection, and feedback-driven composition. It collects strategies from broad external sources, generates new variants through self-reflection and genetic evolution, and retains effective strategies based on their performance against aligned LLMs. During attack execution, DARWIN-Attack adaptively selects and combines evolved strategies according to feedback from target LLMs and guardrails. Across frontier models and guardrails, it achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates, including nearly 100% on DeepSeek-V4-Pro and YuFeng-XGuard and over 90% on GPT-5.5. On the defense side, we introduce DARWIN-Guard, an online adversarial training paradigm that iteratively learns from emerging adversarial samples generated by DARWIN-Attack. To improve robustness without sacrificing utility, DARWIN-Guard jointly trains on malicious and benign disguised queries, encouraging the model to identify underlying intent rather than superficial attack patterns. DARWIN-Guard achieves an average unsafe recall of 91.6% across 12 safety benchmarks, outperforming strong guardrails such as YuFeng-XGuard and Nemotron Guard, while maintaining a nearly 100% pass rate on standard benign datasets.
tldr: This paper proposes an evolutionary attack-defense framework for LLM safety, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Existing LLM safety methods are static and cannot adapt to evolving real-world adversaries.
method: DARWIN uses an evolutionary algorithm to generate jailbreak attacks and an online adversarial training paradigm to update guardrails.
result: DARWIN-Attack achieves near 100% attack success on frontier models, and DARWIN-Guard achieves 91.6% unsafe recall while maintaining benign utility.
conclusion: The evolutionary approach effectively improves LLM safety evaluation and protection against adaptive adversaries.

title: The Dynamic Turn In Paraconsistency
authors: Hans van Ditmarsch Rafael Ongaratto
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work we propose a dynamic turn in paraconsistency. We introduce AMLFI1, the action model extension of the paraconsistent logic LFI1. A special case is PALFI1, a paraconsistent logic of public announcements. It corresponds to another, recently published, paraconsistent public announcement logic: the differences in their axiomatizations are mutually admissible. We also introduce UMLFI1, that extends AMLFI1 with factual change. Soundness and completeness are proven for all logics, and all extend the epistemic paraconsistent logics KLFI1, KB4LFI1 and S5LFI1, known from the literature. With such dynamic epistemic paraconsistent logics we can formalize obtaining and resolving provisional contradictions.
tldr: This paper proposes dynamic epistemic paraconsistent logics for handling provisional contradictions.
motivation: To extend paraconsistent logic with dynamic epistemic operators to model obtaining and resolving contradictions in multi-agent settings.
method: Introduces action model logic AMLFI1 and public announcement logic PALFI1 based on the paraconsistent logic LFI1, with soundness and completeness proofs.
result: All proposed logics are sound and complete, and PALFI1 is shown to be equivalent to another recently published paraconsistent public announcement logic.
conclusion: Dynamic epistemic paraconsistent logics can formalize reasoning with provisional contradictions in epistemic contexts.

title: HijackKV: New Threat In Position-Independent Kv Cache Reuse
authors: Yichi Zhang, Zhiqi Wang, Huan Zhang, Yuchen Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Key-Value (KV) cache reduces inference latency in large language models (LLMs). Traditional prefix-based reuse has low cache hit rates across inference requests because it requires exact token and position matches. To improve efficiency, recent system optimizations introduce position-independent KV reuse, allowing KV cache to be reused whenever identical text chunks appear, regardless of their position in the sequence. We show this design introduces a new threat, KV Cache Hijacking. Since KV caches are retrieved by token match but encode the context in which they were originally computed, the KV tied to a benign-looking token chunk may encode an attacker-controlled prefix. When later reused in a victim query, this contaminated KV silently hijacks the model's behavior, even if no attacker-controlled text appears in the input. We introduce HIJACKKV, the first attack framework that systematically exploits this vulnerability, demonstrating its severity and practicality. HIJACKKV optimizes an attacker-controlled prefix, so that the KV computed for a subsequent common benign text encodes the attacker's goal, while the text remains unchanged for future cache hits. HIJACKKV achieves an average 94% success rate in a single attempt, remains effective under realistic constraints including low hit rates (10%) and frequent recomputation (50%), persists over multi-turn interactions, and transfers across models in black-box settings. We further provide design insights for building secure KV reuse systems.
tldr: This paper identifies a security vulnerability in position-independent KV cache reuse for LLMs and proposes an attack framework.
motivation: Position-independent KV cache reuse improves efficiency but introduces a new threat where attacker-controlled prefixes can hijack model behavior.
method: The authors develop HIJACKKV, an attack that optimizes an attacker-controlled prefix so that the KV cache of a benign text encodes the attacker's goal.
result: HIJACKKV achieves 94% success rate in a single attempt and remains effective under low hit rates and frequent recomputation.
conclusion: The work highlights the need for secure KV cache reuse systems and provides design insights.

title: Identity-Truthful Online Decision-Making
authors: Adar Kantor Tomer Ezra
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Bayesian online selection, a decision-maker observes a sequence of stochastic rewards and must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject each realized value. The rewards come from known distributions, referred to as their identities. Whereas classical prophet inequalities compare online algorithms to the offline optimum, recent work studies information gaps relative to the optimal online algorithm, which knows the identities' arrival order. We introduce a new restriction motivated by identity-independent decision-making: the decision-maker observes the current value but learns its identity only after deciding whether to accept it. We call such algorithms identity-truthful. We define the identity-truthfulness gap as the optimal worst-case approximation achievable by identity-truthful algorithms relative to the optimal online benchmark. This gap lies between the order-competitive ratio [Ezra et al. 2023] and the identity-blindness gap [Ezra et al. 2024]. We design an algorithm establishing that the identity-truthfulness gap is strictly greater than [MATH], thereby separating it from the identity-blindness gap, which is exactly [MATH]. We complement this result with an upper bound of [MATH] on the identity-truthfulness gap, which is strictly lower than the known upper bound of [MATH] on the order-competitive ratio [Chen et al. 2024]. Finally, we study the relationship between identity-truthful algorithms and pricing mechanisms. Motivated by questions on the power of posted prices in prophet inequalities [Duetting et al. 2020], we show that identity-truthfulness breaks the usual connection between online algorithms and pricing: there exists an instance for which the optimal identity-truthful algorithm cannot be implemented by any pricing mechanism.
tldr: This paper studies identity-truthful algorithms in Bayesian online selection, a problem in online decision-making and prophet inequalities.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the information gap between decision-makers who know the identity of a reward only after deciding to accept or reject it, compared to optimal online algorithms.
method: They define the identity-truthfulness gap and design algorithms to bound it, using techniques from online selection and prophet inequalities.
result: They show the identity-truthfulness gap is strictly greater than 1/2 and less than 0.634, separating it from related gaps, and demonstrate that identity-truthful algorithms cannot always be implemented by pricing mechanisms.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into the power of information in online decision-making and its connection to pricing.

title: A SAT-Based Exact Approach For Radio k-Labeling
authors: Huong Vu Thanh, Duc Dao Van, Khanh To van
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The radio [MATH]-labeling (or [MATH]-coloring) problem seeks a minimum-span assignment of nonnegative integer labels to the vertices of a connected graph [MATH] such that [MATH] for all vertex pairs. Although numerous theoretical constructions and some heuristic algorithms have been proposed, existing approaches generally fail to provide certified optimal solutions for broad graph classes. This paper presents an exact SAT-based framework for radio k-labeling that combines a compact order encoding with incremental SAT solving. The proposed framework incrementally tightens the admissible span while reusing learned clauses across SAT calls, avoiding repeated formula reconstruction. Experimental results on 146 benchmark instances from nine graph families demonstrate that the proposed approach establishes 38 new best-known radio numbers while matching or improving the best-known radio numbers on 130 of the 146 benchmark instances. The proposed SAT framework outperforms state-of-the-art commercial optimization solvers, including CPLEX and Gurobi, in terms of overall solution quality, and substantially improves upon previously published heuristic methods. Furthermore, by combining the SAT frameworks with ILP models solved by CPLEX and Gurobi, the study certifies optimal solutions for 109 of the 146 benchmark instances, substantially expanding the set of radio-labeling benchmarks with proven optimality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of incremental SAT solving as a practical exact optimization framework for difficult graph-labeling problems.
tldr: This paper presents a SAT-based exact optimization framework for radio k-labeling on graphs, achieving new best-known results on many benchmarks.
motivation: Radio labeling is a graph labeling problem with applications in frequency assignment, but existing methods often fail to provide certified optimal solutions for broad graph classes.
method: The authors propose a SAT-based framework using compact order encoding and incremental SAT solving, which tightens the admissible span while reusing learned clauses across calls.
result: On 146 benchmark instances from nine graph families, the approach establishes 38 new best-known radio numbers and certifies optimal solutions for 109 instances, outperforming CPLEX and Gurobi.
conclusion: Incremental SAT solving is an effective exact optimization method for difficult graph-labeling problems, substantially expanding the set of benchmarks with proven optimality.

title: What Is A Model Of The Linear Lambda Calculus?
authors: Arturo de Faveri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the notion of model of the linear [MATH]-calculus from an algebraic perspective. Our starting point is the operad of linear [MATH]-terms, whose algebras provide a natural candidate. We prove that this notion of model is equivalent to two other structures: a linear analogue of Curry's [MATH]-algebras, and semiclosed operads, a class of operads equipped with an internal abstraction operation. The equivalence between these three approaches unifies three complementary answers to the question of what should be regarded as a model of the linear [MATH]-calculus. As a second contribution, we give a finite equational presentation for the linear variant of [MATH]-algebras using the linear combinators [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. Finally, exploiting the equivalence with semiclosed operads, we establish a linear analogue of Scott's representation theorem by showing that every model arises as a reflexive object in a natural monoidal closed category of presheaves.
tldr: This paper investigates algebraic models of the linear lambda calculus, unifying three perspectives: linear lambda-term operads, linear Curry algebras, and semiclosed operads.
motivation: The linear lambda calculus is a foundational computational model, but its notion of model was not well-understood from an algebraic viewpoint. The authors aim to provide a unified framework.
method: The paper uses operad theory, algebraic structures, and categorical semantics to define and compare three equivalent notions of model, and provides a finite equational presentation for linear combinators.
result: The three approaches are proven equivalent, and a linear analogue of Scott's representation theorem is established, showing every model arises as a reflexive object in a monoidal closed category of presheaves.
conclusion: The work offers a comprehensive algebraic characterization of models for the linear lambda calculus, unifying existing perspectives and providing a foundation for further study.

title: A Logical 3-valued Semantics For Nondeterministic Choice
authors: Alessandro Aldini (dipartimento Di Scienze Pure E Applicate Universita' Di Urbino, Urbino, Italy), Pierluigi Graziani (dipartimento Di Scienze Pure E Applicate Universita' Di Urbino, Urbino, Italy), Claudio Antares Mezzina (dipartimento Di Scienze Pure E Applicate Universita' Di Urbino, Urbino, Italy), Gandolfo Vergottini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a logical formalisation of computational errors in reactive, nondeterministic systems. To this aim, we introduce a new three-valued symmetric nondeterministic disjunction, designed to provide a faithful logical representation of the nondeterministic choice arising in concurrent computations. The connective is defined within the framework of nondeterministic matrices (Nmatrices) and derives from a minimal combination of Kleene's tolerant semantics and Bochvar's symmetric error persistence, thereby eliminating the residual asymmetry induced by sequential evaluation strategies such as McCarthy's logic. The resulting semantics admits genuinely nondeterministic outcomes in mixed cases involving errors, while preserving commutativity and operational symmetry.
tldr: This paper proposes a three-valued logical semantics for nondeterministic choice in concurrent systems, combining Kleene and Bochvar logics.
motivation: To provide a faithful logical representation of nondeterministic choice in reactive systems that handles computational errors symmetrically.
method: Defines a new three-valued symmetric nondeterministic disjunction within the framework of nondeterministic matrices, derived from Kleene's tolerant semantics and Bochvar's symmetric error persistence.
result: The resulting semantics admits genuinely nondeterministic outcomes in mixed cases involving errors while preserving commutativity and operational symmetry.
conclusion: The proposed logical formalization eliminates residual asymmetry from sequential evaluation strategies like McCarthy's logic.

title: Linearising Explicit Substitutions Using Intersection Types
authors: Ana Jorge Almeida (liacc,faculdade de Ci\^encias Da Universidade Do Porto), Sandra Alves (CRACS, Inesc-Tec,faculdade de Ci\^encias Da Universidade Do Porto), M\'ario Florido
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Term expansion was originally introduced in 2004 as a way to relate terms typed in an intersection type system with linear terms. Recently, new applications of term expansion include the relation of lambda-terms with terms typed in other substructural type systems, such as the relevant and the ordered type systems, and the use of quantitative types to relate the strongly normalising lambda-terms with weak linear terms that share the same normal form. Here we define a new term expansion for a calculus with explicit substitutions, using it to relate a lambda-calculus with explicit substitutions to Boudol's resource aware lambda-calculus with multiplicities, where function arguments have a possibly limited availability.
tldr: This paper introduces a term expansion for a lambda-calculus with explicit substitutions, relating it to a resource-aware lambda-calculus using intersection types.
motivation: To extend the concept of term expansion to calculi with explicit substitutions, enabling connections to substructural type systems and resource-aware computation.
method: Defines a new term expansion for a lambda-calculus with explicit substitutions and uses it to relate the calculus to Boudol's resource-aware lambda-calculus with multiplicities.
result: Establishes a relationship between explicit substitution calculi and resource-aware lambda-calculi via intersection types.
conclusion: The work provides a framework for understanding explicit substitutions in the context of resource-aware computation and type systems.

title: Basic Model Theory For Path Predicate Modal Logic
authors: Raul Fervari (conicet,universidad Nacional de Cordoba Argentina), Santiago Figueira (conicet,universidad de Buenos Aires Argentina), Gabriel Goren-Roig (conicet,universidad de Buenos Aires Argentina), Leonardo Torres
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Path Predicate Modal Logic (PPML) is a generalization of Basic Modal Logic, where atoms are relational predicates instead of propositional symbols. The study of PPML is motivated as a way to abstractly investigate data-aware formalisms, such as XPath or DataGL. In this paper, we investigate some basic model theoretical aspects of PPML to better characterize its expressive power. More concretely, we investigate different ways of defining Hennessy-Milner classes, and a van Benthem characterization theorem. In doing so, we discuss the main challenges of dealing with the novel features of PPML, and what are the similarities with the standard approaches.
tldr: This paper develops model theory for Path Predicate Modal Logic, a generalization of basic modal logic with relational predicates.
motivation: To better characterize the expressive power of PPML, which abstracts data-aware formalisms like XPath and DataGL.
method: Investigates Hennessy-Milner classes and a van Benthem characterization theorem for PPML, discussing challenges and similarities with standard approaches.
result: Provides foundational model-theoretic results for PPML, including characterizations of expressive power.
conclusion: The work advances understanding of PPML's model theory, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: MaudeTypedLog: A Typed Interpreter For Prolog In Maude
authors: Enrique Gallifa-Tronch (valencian Research Institute For Artificial Intelligence), Jo\~ao Barbosa (DCC, Faculdade de Ci\^encias Da Universidade Do Porto), Santiago Escobar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prolog is traditionally thought of as an untyped logic programming language, although there are queries that result in a type error. Several attempts of statically introducing a type discipline in Prolog have been made but they have not been widely adopted. We use Maude to implement a typed unification algorithm and use it as the basis for an interpreter for Prolog called MaudeTypedLog. This interpreter follows the Typed SLD-resolution operational semantics for logic programming, that makes it possible to detect type errors in both programs and queries dynamically.
tldr: This paper presents a typed interpreter for Prolog implemented in Maude, focusing on dynamic type error detection via typed unification.
motivation: Prolog lacks a widely adopted type system, leading to runtime type errors; the authors aim to provide a typed operational semantics to detect such errors dynamically.
method: They implement a typed unification algorithm in Maude and use it as the basis for an interpreter that follows Typed SLD-resolution operational semantics.
result: The interpreter can detect type errors in both programs and queries during execution.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical approach to adding type checking to Prolog without requiring static type annotations.

title: Phase Semantic Cut-elimination For Intuitionistic Linear Logic With Least And Greatest Fixed Points
authors: Jun Suzuki (hokkaido University), Charles Grellois (university Of Sheffield), Katsuhiko Sano
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes the cut-elimination theorem for intuitionistic propositional multiplicative-additive linear logic with the least and greatest fixpoints ([MATH]IMALL) by means of its phase semantics. A classical first-order multiplicative-additive linear logic system with the least and greatest fixpoints was introduced by Baelde and Miller (2007). Its intuitionistic fragment was discussed in Baelde (2012), but the cut-elimination theorem for this fragment has not yet been proved. We introduce a propositional fragment of this system, [MATH]IMALL, and establish the cut-elimination theorem. To prove the theorem, we define phase semantics for [MATH]IMALL and show the following two statements: (1) Soundness: if a formula is provable in [MATH]IMALL, then it is true in all phase models, and (2) Cut-free Completeness: if a formula is true in all phase models, then it is provable in [MATH]IMALL without Cut. Okada (1999, 2002) employed a phase semantic method to prove the cut-elimination theorems for classical and intuitionistic linear logic systems. De et al. (2022) applied this method to a propositional fragment of classical propositional multiplicative-additive linear logic with the least and greatest fixpoints. We refine and apply their arguments to prove the cut-elimination theorem for [MATH]IMALL.
tldr: This paper proves cut-elimination for intuitionistic linear logic with fixed points using phase semantics.
motivation: The cut-elimination theorem for intuitionistic linear logic with fixed points had not been proved, and this work fills that gap.
method: The authors define phase semantics for the logic and prove soundness and cut-free completeness, adapting techniques from Okada and De et al.
result: They establish that every provable formula is true in all phase models and that every formula true in all phase models is provable without cut.
conclusion: The cut-elimination theorem holds for the intuitionistic fragment of multiplicative-additive linear logic with least and greatest fixed points.
